Rules summary Contents 1 Arabella - Quick Rules 1.1 Overview 1.2 Gameplay 1.3 Main Actions 1.4 Scoring Arabella - Quick Rules Overview Players: 1 to 4 players. Objective: Collect the most Victory Points (VP) by building tracks, purchasing trains, and investing in company shares. Game End: Triggered when the last "6" train is purchased or a player reaches the end of their money track. Gameplay The game is played over several rounds using a shared pool of 6 dice. On your turn, you must take all dice of a single value (e.g., all available 4s) from the pool to perform one action. Select Dice: Take all dice of one value. Modifiers (Optional): Use unlocked abilities to change the value by +/- 1. Perform Action: The number of dice taken determines the strength/quantity of the action, while the value often determines the type. Main Actions Take Income: Mark spaces on your money track based on the number of dice taken. Reaching milestones unlocks permanent bonuses or special abilities. Build Track: The die value determines the shape of the track (straight, curve, etc.), and the number of dice determines how many sections you draw on your map. Buy Trains: Use money to purchase locomotives and cars. The number of dice determines how many units you buy; the value determines the tech level (range). New tech levels eventually make older trains obsolete. Buy Shares: Invest in rail companies. The share price is equal to the total number of train units currently owned by that company. Shares provide dividends and end-game VPs. Run Trains: Activate your rail lines to generate cash. You receive income for cities in your route, and other shareholders of that company receive dividends. Scoring At the end of the game, points are awarded for: Total value of your shares (Quantity x current share price). Completed target cards (Contracts). Unlocked bonuses on your player board. Remaining cash (usually at a lower conversion rate).

[Rating: 1/10] The dice pool rules completely derail this game. In the first few rounds, player one gets 3 dice, player two gets 2, and players three and four are left with just one die each. This imbalance is brutal—whoever starts strong quickly snowballs, owning more shares, earning more cash, and laying down more track while the others are left in the dust. It’s a wild, unbalanced ride.  On the bright side (if you can call it that), the game only takes about 5 to 12 minutes to play, because that’s how long it takes to spot the clear winner—usually the player who just happened to go first. [Rating: 3/10] The game offers a unique design and interesting concepts but seems to be problematic in terms of game rules, complexity, and logic. It lacks essential player aids, and the rules can be intricate and confusing. Achieving the game's end condition might prove difficult, and there are  some balance issues.

[Rating: 3/10] Rating -- Lowered Rating to AVOID.  The game can be lost on the first die roll. (Start player rolls three of a kind, builds three tracks for free ... now all track builds cost, and other players only earn $1 for a single die while start player earns up to $4 for a single die).  The rest of the rules don't work well either.

[Rating: 4/10] The rulebook is awful and very hard to read. Once you get past that there's an ok game hidden in there.  Loads of things make no sense. There are six companies, but only a maximum of four players. The other two companies aren't used and you can't buy stocks from them.  The track placement mechanism is extremely restrictive.  You have multiple trains but you can't place more station tokens? Why?  You can't interact with your opponents' tracks? Again, why?  Lots of strange decisions made. If the game had had another year of development I'm sure it would've been fantastic.
